subject: biology

items.q: Which statement about a population is correct?
items.correct: Its members belong to one species, live in the same area and normally breed with one another.
items.misconception: It includes every member of a species, wherever in the world that species is found.
items.why: In everyday and news usage 'population' is attached to a whole species ('the global tiger population'), and students carry that meaning into ecology without noticing that the IB definition is tied to an area and to interbreeding. A population is an interacting group of organisms of the same species living in an area. Members of a population normally breed with each other, and reproductive isolation is used to distinguish one population of a species from another, so one species usually comprises many populations.
items.specStatementText: A population is one species, one area, interbreeding
items.random_wrong: It includes all the organisms of every species that interact within one area.

items.q: Two groups of great crested newts breed in ponds 5 km apart, and no newt ever moves between the ponds. How should the two groups be described?
items.correct: Two populations of one species, because the groups are reproductively isolated from each other.
items.misconception: Two species, because groups that do not interbreed cannot belong to the same species.
items.why: Students meet 'reproductive isolation' first in the context of speciation, where it means an inability to produce fertile offspring, and assume it has the same meaning when used to distinguish populations. Reproductive isolation between populations means only that interbreeding does not normally happen, usually because the groups are separated geographically. The individuals remain the same species and could interbreed if the separation were removed; that is what distinguishes populations from species.
items.specStatementText: A population is one species, one area, interbreeding
items.random_wrong: One population, because all the newts belong to the same species, wherever they breed.

items.q: Why do ecologists usually estimate the size of a population rather than counting every individual?
items.correct: Counting every individual is usually impractical and may damage the habitat or disturb the organisms.
items.misconception: A large enough random sample gives the true population size exactly, so a complete count is unnecessary.
items.why: Students learn a set of rules for good sampling (random placement, many quadrats) and conclude that following the rules guarantees a correct result, rather than a result that is close on average. Random sampling, instead of measuring an entire population, inevitably results in sampling error: the difference between the estimate and the true size of the whole population. Increasing the sample size makes the error smaller on average but cannot eliminate it.
items.specStatementText: Estimate by random sampling, and accept sampling error
items.random_wrong: Sampling lets the investigator select the most typical parts of the habitat in which to count.

items.q: A student uses random quadrats to estimate that a rocky shore holds 420 limpets. A later complete count finds 460. Which statement about the sampling error is correct?
items.correct: It is 40 limpets, and arose because only a sample of the shore was measured, not all of it.
items.misconception: It is 40 limpets, and arose from mistakes the student made when counting inside the quadrats.
items.why: In everyday language an 'error' is a blunder, and school practical work stresses 'sources of error' as things the student did wrong, so the technical meaning of sampling error is lost. Sampling error is inevitable even with perfect technique: a random sample can, by chance, contain more or fewer individuals per unit area than the population as a whole. The IB defines it as the difference between the estimate of population size and the true size of the whole population.
items.specStatementText: Estimate by random sampling, and accept sampling error
items.random_wrong: It would have been zero if the student had placed enough quadrats to sample the shore properly.

items.q: A student places ten 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrats at random in a 250 m² meadow and counts 20 orchids in total. What is the estimated population of orchids in the meadow?
items.correct: 2000 plants
items.misconception: 20 plants
items.why: Counting is what the student actually does in the field, so the count feels like the result; the scaling-up step is done later on paper and is easily forgotten. Random quadrat sampling gives an estimate of density. Population size = mean number per quadrat ÷ quadrat area × total area of the habitat. The sample count is only a small fraction of the population.
items.specStatementText: Quadrats for things that stay put
items.random_wrong: 500 plants

items.q: Limpets were counted in twenty random quadrats on each of two shores. On both shores the mean was 8 limpets per quadrat. The standard deviation was 1.2 on shore A and 6.5 on shore B. What can be concluded?
items.correct: Limpets on shore B are distributed less evenly, because the counts varied much more from quadrat to quadrat.
items.misconception: Shore B has a larger limpet population than shore A, because its standard deviation is higher.
items.why: Students treat any larger statistic as meaning 'more of the thing measured', and have not separated a measure of spread from a measure of central value. Two populations can have the same mean number per quadrat but different standard deviations: the one with the larger standard deviation is spread less evenly, not more numerous.
items.specStatementText: Quadrats for things that stay put
items.random_wrong: The sampling on shore B was carried out incorrectly, so its mean of 8 per quadrat is not valid.

items.q: In a capture–mark–release–recapture study, 40 woodlice were caught, marked and released. Later, 50 woodlice were caught, of which 10 were marked. What is the Lincoln index estimate of the population?
items.correct: About 200
items.misconception: About 8
items.why: The formula is often learned as a string of symbols rather than derived from the proportion argument, so there is nothing to stop the letters being rearranged under exam pressure. If R of the N recaptured individuals are marked, the fraction marked is R/N. That same fraction of the whole population was marked, and M individuals were marked, so the population is M ÷ (R/N) = M × N ÷ R. A smaller R means marked individuals are more diluted, so the population is larger.
items.specStatementText: Mark, release, recapture for things that move
items.random_wrong: About 2000

items.q: Beetles were marked with a spot of bright paint that made them easier for birds to see. Compared with the true population size, what will the Lincoln index estimate be, and why?
items.correct: Too high, because fewer marked beetles survive to be recaptured, so R is too small.
items.misconception: Too low, because fewer marked beetles are recaptured and fewer recaptures mean a smaller population.
items.why: Students reason by direct proportion, 'fewer recaptured, fewer animals', without recognising that R is in the denominator and that a low R signals that the marked animals were heavily diluted. The method assumes marks do not affect survival or the chance of recapture. If marked individuals are lost, the marked fraction in the second sample under-represents the true fraction, so the population is overestimated.
items.specStatementText: Mark, release, recapture for things that move
items.random_wrong: Unaffected, provided the second sample is taken at the release point soon after the beetles are released.

items.q: Which statement gives the meaning of the carrying capacity of an environment for a species?
items.correct: The maximum population size that the resources available in the environment can support sustainably over time.
items.misconception: The number of individuals that can physically fit into the area that the population occupies.
items.why: 'Capacity' in everyday English means room to fit things in, so students picture the habitat filling up physically rather than its resources being used up. Carrying capacity is limited by resources: food, water, light, mineral nutrients, territory, nesting or shelter sites. Space is only one such resource, and populations normally stop growing long before the area is physically full.
items.specStatementText: Carrying capacity is set by limited resources
items.random_wrong: The greatest number of offspring that each individual of the species is able to produce in its lifetime.

items.q: A storm kills 30% of a seabird colony. Over the following years, the colony returns to its former size. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: The storm was density-independent; reduced competition afterwards let natality exceed mortality until carrying capacity was regained.
items.misconception: The storm was a density-dependent factor, because it killed so many birds in a colony as large as this one was.
items.why: Students judge by the number of deaths rather than by the proportion, and a bigger population inevitably has more deaths from any cause, so every factor looks density-dependent. Density-independent factors such as extreme weather affect the same proportion regardless of density, so they cause fluctuations but do not push the population back towards the carrying capacity. Density-dependent factors, such as competition for limited resources, predation and the transfer of pathogens or pests, affect a larger proportion as density rises.
items.specStatementText: Density-dependent factors push numbers back towards carrying capacity
items.random_wrong: Density-dependent factors can only ever reduce populations, so the recovery afterwards must have been due to density-independent factors.

items.q: Which statement about density-dependent factors is correct?
items.correct: The proportion of individuals they kill or prevent from breeding rises as the population becomes more dense.
items.misconception: Predation and disease are density-independent, since predators and pathogens come from outside the population.
items.why: Competition is the first and most emphasised example of a density-dependent factor, and students draw the line between 'internal' and 'external' causes instead of between proportion-dependent and proportion-independent effects. The guide names three density-dependent factors: competition for limited resources, the increased risk of predation in dense populations, and the transfer of pathogens or pests between individuals living close together.
items.specStatementText: Density-dependent factors push numbers back towards carrying capacity
items.random_wrong: Any factor that kills more individuals when the population is larger, including a flood or a frost, is density-dependent.

items.q: Why is the growth of a population exponential in its initial phase?
items.correct: Resources are plentiful, so most individuals survive to reproduce.
items.misconception: Each individual reproduces faster and faster as the phase continues.
items.why: Students see the population growth rate rising and attribute it to individuals speeding up, confusing the population's growth rate with the per-individual rate of reproduction, which stays roughly constant. In exponential growth the per-capita rates of natality and mortality are constant; the growth accelerates because a constant proportional increase is applied to an ever-larger number of individuals.
items.specStatementText: The sigmoid curve is a model, and real populations can overshoot it
items.random_wrong: Individuals reach maturity sooner than they will later at higher density.

items.q: A student records the size of a duckweed population every two days and plots it on a logarithmic vertical axis against time on a non-logarithmic horizontal axis. Which observation would show that growth was exponential?
items.correct: The points lie on a straight line, because the population multiplied by the same factor in each two-day interval.
items.misconception: The points form a curve that becomes steeper with time, as exponential growth does on ordinary axes.
items.why: Students have only seen exponential growth on ordinary axes and treat the J shape as the definition of exponential growth, rather than as one representation of it; logarithmic axes are unfamiliar. The test for exponential growth is to plot population size on a logarithmic vertical axis against time on a non-logarithmic horizontal axis. Exponential growth gives a straight line; a line that bends over shows growth is slowing.
items.specStatementText: The sigmoid curve is a model, and real populations can overshoot it
items.random_wrong: The points lie on a straight line, because a fixed number of plants was added in each two-day interval.

items.q: In 1911, 25 reindeer were introduced to St Paul Island, Alaska, where they had almost no predators. By 1938 there were about 2000; by 1950 only 8 remained, after the lichens they ate in winter had been destroyed. How should this be interpreted in relation to the sigmoid growth model?
items.correct: The model is a simplification: the reindeer overshot the carrying capacity because their food was destroyed faster than it regrew.
items.misconception: The reindeer must have levelled off at a plateau at some point between 1938 and 1950 that the counts simply failed to record properly.
items.why: Textbook graphs are presented as smooth and authoritative, and students are rarely shown the messy field data that the curve simplifies, so the model is mistaken for the reality. NOS: models are often simplifications of complex systems. The sigmoid curve captures the general pattern of exponential growth followed by a plateau, but a real population's deviations from it are real information about factors the model leaves out.
items.specStatementText: The sigmoid curve is a model, and real populations can overshoot it
items.random_wrong: The crash shows that the carrying capacity of reindeer is fixed at about 2000 animals, wherever they live.

items.q: Yeast was grown in a sealed flask of glucose solution and cell counts were made every four hours. After 24 hours the count stopped rising. Which explanation for the plateau is correct?
items.correct: Natality now equals mortality, because glucose has become scarce and ethanol has accumulated.
items.misconception: The yeast cells have all stopped dividing, and none of them are dying, so the count stays the same.
items.why: A horizontal line on a graph is read as inactivity, and students do not distinguish a static population from a dynamic balance between opposite processes. At the plateau the population is at its carrying capacity: density-dependent factors have raised mortality and lowered natality until the two are balanced, so numbers stay roughly constant while individuals are still being born and dying.
items.specStatementText: Growing a population in the lab
items.random_wrong: The plateau is reached only at the moment when the glucose in the flask has been completely used up.

items.q: Which pair gives one example of intraspecific competition followed by one example of intraspecific cooperation?
items.correct: Oak seedlings shading each other; meerkats taking turns as sentinels.
items.misconception: Grey squirrels taking acorns from red squirrels; wolves hunting together as a pack.
items.why: Familiar images of animals of one species are herds, flocks and packs, and 'competition' is usually introduced with two different species, so within-species competition goes unnoticed. Intraspecific competition occurs within a population precisely because its members have identical requirements. Competition and cooperation both occur within species, and the same population may show both at different times.
items.specStatementText: Same species: compete and cooperate
items.random_wrong: Sardines swimming together in a shoal; emperor penguins huddling against the cold.

items.q: Which description of a community is correct?
items.correct: All the populations of plants, animals, fungi and bacteria that live and interact in an area.
items.misconception: All the populations of plants and animals, but not microorganisms, that live in an area.
items.why: Fungi and bacteria are invisible in the habitats students study, and food-web diagrams typically show only plants and animals, so decomposers and microorganisms are left out of the mental picture. The community is all of the interacting organisms in an ecosystem. Fungi and bacteria are populations in their own right and interact with the other populations as decomposers, pathogens and mutualistic partners.
items.specStatementText: A community is all the living things in an ecosystem
items.random_wrong: All the organisms in an area together with the soil, water and climate they depend on.

items.q: A tick attaches to a deer and feeds on its blood for several days before dropping off. Which category of interspecific relationship is this?
items.correct: Parasitism, because the tick takes nutrition from a living host without killing it.
items.misconception: Predation, because the tick is an animal feeding on the body of another animal.
items.why: Both relationships involve one organism gaining food at another's expense, and everyday language uses 'preys on' loosely, so the distinction between killing and living off a host is not made. Predation and parasitism are separate categories of interspecific relationship. The defining difference is that a predator kills and consumes the prey, whereas a parasite exploits a living host, typically much larger than itself, without directly killing it.
items.specStatementText: Six ways species interact
items.random_wrong: Pathogenicity, because the tick is a small organism that harms a much larger one.

items.q: What are the benefits to each partner in the relationship between a legume and the bacteria in its root nodules?
items.correct: The bacteria supply the plant with fixed nitrogen as ammonia or amino acids; the plant supplies the bacteria with sugars.
items.misconception: The bacteria supply the plant with nitrogen gas from the soil; the plant supplies the bacteria with oxygen.
items.why: 'Plants need nitrogen' is learned before the chemistry of nitrogen fixation, and the word 'nitrogen' is used loosely for the element, the gas and nitrate, so the crucial conversion of unreactive N₂ is missed. Nitrogen gas is unreactive and unusable by plants. Rhizobium bacteria in the nodules fix it into ammonia, and the plant receives it as ammonium or amino acids. In return the plant supplies the bacteria with sugars from photosynthesis and a protected environment in the nodule.
items.specStatementText: Mutualism: both partners gain
items.random_wrong: The plant gains fixed nitrogen from the bacteria; the bacteria gain nothing from the plant but are not harmed by living in the nodule.

items.q: When sea temperatures rise, hard corals expel their zooxanthellae, turn white and often die of starvation within weeks. Why does losing the algae starve the coral?
items.correct: The coral loses the sugars and other carbon compounds the algae made by photosynthesis.
items.misconception: The coral can no longer photosynthesize, because the algae carried its chlorophyll for it.
items.why: Hard corals are brightly coloured, fixed in place and confined to shallow sunlit water, all features associated with plants, and their algal partners are hidden inside their cells. The coral's dependence on light is a consequence of the mutualism: zooxanthellae photosynthesize and release sugars and other carbon compounds to the coral, while the coral provides a protected, sunlit position, carbon dioxide and nitrogen-containing waste such as ammonium.
items.specStatementText: Mutualism: both partners gain
items.random_wrong: The coral loses the shelter and the carbon dioxide that the algae had been providing for it.

items.q: The grey squirrel was introduced to Britain from North America in the nineteenth century and has replaced the endemic red squirrel across most of England and Wales. Which statement correctly describes the competitive advantage in resource acquisition that underlies this invasion?
items.correct: Grey squirrels digest unripe acorns and store more fat, so they take a larger share of the shared food supply and out-reproduce red squirrels.
items.misconception: Grey squirrels kill red squirrels and their young in fights, so red squirrels are driven out of any wood the greys enter.
items.why: Media coverage of invasions stresses aggression and dramatic damage, and students picture a contest rather than a quieter difference in efficiency at using resources. The grey squirrel in Britain did not need to attack red squirrels: it is larger, stores more body fat, and can digest unripe acorns that red squirrels cannot, so it takes more of the shared food supply and its population grows while the red squirrel's declines.
items.specStatementText: Invasive species win the competition for resources
items.random_wrong: Red squirrels, being adapted to British woodland, hold their ground wherever food is scarce, so greys spread only where food is plentiful.

items.q: On a rocky shore, barnacle species A is found on the lower shore only where barnacle species B is absent. When B is scraped from some plots on the lower shore, A colonises them and grows well. What can be concluded?
items.correct: Competition is indicated but not proven, because A's success could depend on other factors that differ where B is absent.
items.misconception: The initial survey of where A and B occur was an experiment, so by itself it establishes that they compete.
items.why: In school 'doing an experiment' is used for any practical activity, so the defining feature of an experiment, manipulation of a variable, is never isolated. NOS: hypotheses can be tested by both experiments and observations. Field observation by random sampling, laboratory experiments and field manipulation by removing one species are all valid approaches; only the last two are experiments.
items.specStatementText: Testing for competition: experiment or observation
items.random_wrong: Interspecific competition between A and B is proven, because A colonises and grows well in every single plot from which B was removed.

items.q: Ecologists want to test the hypothesis that two limpet species compete for algae on a shore. Which approach tests the hypothesis by experiment rather than by observation?
items.correct: Removing one limpet species from marked plots and recording the growth of the other over a year.
items.misconception: Measuring the shell sizes of both limpet species in laboratory tanks of seawater collected from the shore.
items.why: Most school experiments happen in a laboratory and most fieldwork is surveying, so location becomes the cue for the category. Field manipulation by removal of one species is one of the experimental approaches the guide names for testing competition. Whether an investigation is an experiment depends on the deliberate change of a variable, not on where it takes place.
items.specStatementText: Testing for competition: experiment or observation
items.random_wrong: Recording the abundance of both limpet species in quadrats placed at random positions along the shore.

items.q: Fur records from the Hudson's Bay Company show snowshoe hare and Canada lynx numbers rising and falling in cycles of about ten years, with each peak in lynx numbers occurring one to two years after a peak in hares. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Abundant hares let more lynx survive and breed, so lynx rise later; more lynx then reduce hares, after which lynx decline and hares recover.
items.misconception: Lynx and hare numbers should peak at the same time, so the delay of one to two years shows that the fur records were unreliable.
items.why: Students expect an immediate cause-and-effect link and overlook that predators take time to breed and rear young in response to a food supply, and time to starve when it disappears. In the Hudson's Bay Company fur records, lynx peaks follow snowshoe hare peaks by one to two years. More hares allow more lynx to survive and breed; the larger lynx population then drives hare numbers down; lynx then decline, and hares recover.
items.specStatementText: Predator and prey numbers cycle, with the predator lagging
items.random_wrong: The lynx eat nearly all the hares, so each crash is followed by a period with no lynx at all until new ones immigrate into the area.

items.q: After sea otters were hunted almost to extinction along parts of the North Pacific coast, sea urchin numbers increased greatly and the kelp forests were grazed away. Which statement about population control in this community is correct?
items.correct: Top-down control is dominant: the predator limited the herbivore, which in turn limited the producer below it.
items.misconception: Neither type of control is shown, because otters do not eat kelp and so their loss cannot have affected it.
items.why: Students consider single links of a food chain in isolation and do not trace the consequences of a change across two or more links. When sea otters were removed from parts of the North Pacific coast, sea urchin numbers rose and kelp forests were grazed away, an example of top-down control passing from predator through herbivore to producer.
items.specStatementText: Control can come from the top or the bottom
items.random_wrong: Top-down control is shown, which demonstrates that nutrient supply plays no part in limiting this community.

items.q: In what way are allelopathy in plants and the secretion of antibiotics by microorganisms similar?
items.correct: In both, a chemical substance is released into the surroundings to deter potential competitors.
items.misconception: In both, a chemical is released to destroy pathogens that would otherwise cause disease in the producer.
items.why: Antibiotics are first met as medicines prescribed for bacterial infections, and their ecological origin as weapons in competition between microorganisms is never mentioned. Secretion of antibiotics, like allelopathy, is the release of a chemical into the environment to deter potential competitors. Penicillium moulds secrete penicillin, which stops bacteria growing on the same food; humans later exploited this for medicine.
items.specStatementText: Chemical warfare against competitors
items.random_wrong: In both, a chemical is released as a defence against the animals that would otherwise eat the producer.

items.q: Very few plants grow beneath a black walnut tree, and bacteria fail to grow close to a colony of Penicillium mould on a piece of bread. Which option correctly names the two processes?
items.correct: Allelopathy by the walnut tree; secretion of an antibiotic by the mould.
items.misconception: Defence against herbivores by the walnut; antibiotic secretion by the mould.
items.why: Plant chemical defences against herbivores are a familiar idea, so any toxic plant chemical is assumed to be aimed at animals rather than at neighbouring plants. Black walnut releases juglone from its roots and fallen leaves, which suppresses many plants growing beneath it. The target is potential competitors for resources, which is what makes allelopathy comparable to antibiotic secretion by microorganisms.
items.specStatementText: Chemical warfare against competitors
items.random_wrong: Allelopathy by the walnut; treatment of the bread's bacterial disease by the mould.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the exchange between an orchid and its mycorrhizal fungus?
items.correct: The fungus supplies mineral ions and, to the seedling, carbon compounds; the photosynthesizing orchid supplies sugars.
items.misconception: The fungus fixes nitrogen gas into ammonia for the orchid; the orchid supplies the fungus with sugars made in photosynthesis.
items.why: Both are root mutualisms with a microorganism, taught together, so their benefits are merged into one 'root partner gives nitrogen' idea. Root nodules: bacteria fix nitrogen gas into ammonia and amino acids. Mycorrhizae: fungal hyphae extend the root system, absorbing mineral ions such as phosphate and water; in orchids the fungus also feeds the seedling with carbon compounds because the tiny seed has no reserves.
items.specStatementText: Mutualism: both partners gain
items.random_wrong: The fungus takes sugars from the orchid's roots and the orchid gains nothing in return, so the fungus is really a parasite.

items.q: Two lichen species were recorded as present or absent in 80 random quadrats on a stone wall: both present 16, only A present 32, only B present 24, neither 8. If the two species were distributed independently of each other, how many quadrats would be expected to contain both species?
items.correct: 24 quadrats
items.misconception: 16 quadrats
items.why: Students read the raw 'both present' count as the answer and skip the comparison with the expected frequency, which is the whole point of the test. Expected frequency = (row total × column total) ÷ grand total. A negative association, with observed co-occurrence below expected, may provide evidence for interspecific competition; a positive association suggests shared requirements or a beneficial relationship.
items.specStatementText: Chi-squared for association between two species
items.random_wrong: 20 quadrats

items.q: Why does competition occur between members of the same population?
items.correct: Individuals of one species have identical needs, so when a resource is scarce what one uses leaves less for others.
items.misconception: It occurs only when two individuals confront each other over the same item of food, the same mate or the same nesting site.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'competition' is a direct contest between rivals, and dramatic footage of animals fighting reinforces it, so quiet depletion of a shared resource is not recognised as competition. Two plant species drawing on the same soil water, or two squirrel species eating the same acorns at different times, are competing. Competition is about shared use of a limited resource, not about contact.
items.specStatementText: Same species: compete and cooperate
items.random_wrong: It does not occur: members of one species share their resources, and competition arises only between different species.

items.q: Does a population include all the organisms living in an area?
items.correct: No. A population is restricted to one species; all the interacting populations of different species in an area make up a community.
items.misconception: A population is all the organisms living together in one place, whatever species they belong to.
items.why: The everyday sense of a town's 'population' is everyone living there, and students transfer this to habitats, blurring the distinction between a population (one species) and a community (all species). A population is a group of organisms of the same species living in an area. All the populations of different species living and interacting in an ecosystem together form the community.
items.specStatementText: A population is one species, one area, interbreeding
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is it acceptable to choose sampling sites that look typical of the habitat?
items.correct: No. Sites must be chosen at random, for example by generating coordinates from random numbers, so that every part of the area has an equal chance of being sampled and the investigator's judgement cannot bias the estimate.
items.misconception: Choosing quadrat positions that look representative, or throwing the quadrat over your shoulder, is as good as random sampling.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'random' is 'haphazard', and choosing typical-looking sites feels more sensible than trusting chance, so students do not see that human choice introduces bias. Randomness in sampling procedures is needed to avoid bias. Deliberately chosen sites tend to be those where organisms are obvious or easy to count, which biases the estimate; random numbers used as coordinates give every location an equal chance of selection.
items.specStatementText: Estimate by random sampling, and accept sampling error
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the mean count per quadrat be multiplied straight by the area of the habitat in square metres?
items.correct: Only if the quadrat has an area of 1 m². Otherwise the mean count must first be divided by the quadrat's area to give a density per square metre.
items.misconception: A quadrat always represents one square metre, so the mean number per quadrat is the number per square metre.
items.why: Textbook worked examples almost always use 1 m² quadrats, so students never practise converting from a smaller quadrat such as 0.5 m × 0.5 m (0.25 m²). Density = mean number per quadrat ÷ area of one quadrat. A 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrat has an area of 0.25 m², so a mean of 2 per quadrat is a density of 8 per square metre.
items.specStatementText: Quadrats for things that stay put
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is density calculated from the total count in several quadrats?
items.correct: Density = total number counted ÷ total area sampled, where the total area sampled is the number of quadrats multiplied by the area of one quadrat.
items.misconception: Density is the total number counted in all the quadrats divided by the area of a single quadrat.
items.why: Students remember 'number divided by area' and substitute the one area they know, the quadrat's, without recognising that the count came from many quadrats. The area that produced the count is the whole sampled area. Either divide the total count by (number of quadrats × quadrat area), or first find the mean per quadrat and divide that by the quadrat area; both give the same density.
items.specStatementText: Quadrats for things that stay put
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does a large standard deviation of the mean number per quadrat tell you?
items.correct: That the counts vary widely between quadrats, so the population is unevenly spread, with some quadrats containing many individuals and others few. It is a measure of how patchy the distribution is, not a verdict on whether the sampling was done correctly.
items.misconception: A large standard deviation means the sampling was done badly or the mean is invalid.
items.why: 'Deviation' sounds like a fault, and school practical work presents variation between repeats as something to be minimised, so students read a large spread as a sign that the method failed. The standard deviation of the mean number of individuals per quadrat gives a measure of the variation and how evenly the population is spread. A clumped population gives a large standard deviation even when the sampling is perfect; it is information about the population, not about the quality of the work.
items.specStatementText: Quadrats for things that stay put
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the population estimate just the number of different individuals seen in the two samples?
items.correct: No. The estimate uses the proportion of marked individuals in the second sample to infer how many individuals were never caught at all; it is normally far larger than the number actually handled.
items.misconception: The population estimate is the number of distinct individuals encountered, M plus the unmarked ones in the second sample.
items.why: Counting what you have seen is the intuitive way to estimate a number, and students do not recognise that the method is designed to count the individuals that were never seen. The Lincoln index M × N ÷ R estimates the whole population, including individuals never captured. Adding up the individuals encountered gives only a minimum, and misses the point of the proportional reasoning.
items.specStatementText: Mark, release, recapture for things that move
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Should the second sample be taken as soon as possible after release, at the release point?
items.correct: No. Enough time must be allowed for the marked individuals to mix randomly back into the population, and the second sample should be taken across the same area as the first, not just at the release point.
items.misconception: Recapturing straight away, where the animals were released, gives the best estimate because more marked animals are found.
items.why: Students think of recapturing marked animals as the aim of the exercise, and so try to maximise R, rather than seeing R as a measure of how far the marked animals have been diluted. An assumption of the method is that marked individuals mix randomly with the unmarked. If they are recaptured before mixing, R is inflated, and M × N ÷ R underestimates the population.
items.specStatementText: Mark, release, recapture for things that move
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is carrying capacity a fixed characteristic of a species?
items.correct: No. Carrying capacity is the maximum population size a particular environment can support sustainably, so it is set by the resources of that environment and changes if they change.
items.misconception: Each species has its own carrying capacity, fixed by how fast it breeds, that is the same wherever it lives.
items.why: Students encounter 'the carrying capacity for rabbits is 500' in worked examples and read the number as a property of rabbits, rather than of that meadow at that time. Carrying capacity depends on the availability of limiting resources such as food, water, light, space, mineral nutrients or nesting sites in the environment. The same species has different carrying capacities in different habitats, and a habitat's carrying capacity can rise or fall.
items.specStatementText: Carrying capacity is set by limited resources
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does negative feedback mean the population keeps getting smaller?
items.correct: No. Negative feedback means that a change is opposed: a population above the carrying capacity is pushed down, and one below it is allowed to rise, so numbers return towards the carrying capacity.
items.misconception: Negative feedback is a process that always reduces a population, so it is a bad thing for the population.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'negative' is 'bad' or 'downward', so students read negative feedback as a downward pressure rather than as a corrective one that can act in either direction. Density-dependent factors tend to push the population back towards the carrying capacity. When numbers are high, competition, predation and disease increase mortality; when numbers are low, these pressures ease and the population grows. Both are negative feedback.
items.specStatementText: Density-dependent factors push numbers back towards carrying capacity
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What allows a population to recover after its numbers fall well below the carrying capacity?
items.correct: No. Their effect weakens when density is low, so a population below the carrying capacity experiences less competition, predation and disease and is able to grow. They act in both directions to return the population towards the carrying capacity.
items.misconception: After a crash a population recovers because of favourable density-independent conditions such as good weather, not because density-dependent pressures have relaxed.
items.why: Density-dependent factors are introduced as things that 'limit' or 'check' growth, so students think of them as brakes only, not as the mechanism of recovery. Negative feedback control works because the same factors that intensify at high density relax at low density. Reduced competition and predation after a decline allow natality to exceed mortality until the carrying capacity is reached again.
items.specStatementText: Density-dependent factors push numbers back towards carrying capacity
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In a closed culture of yeast, does growth slow only when the glucose is used up?
items.correct: No. Growth slows before the glucose is exhausted, as it becomes scarcer per cell, and other density-dependent factors act at the same time, such as the accumulation of ethanol and other waste products and the fall in pH.
items.misconception: Food is the only thing that limits a population in a culture, and growth continues at full speed until it has completely run out.
items.why: Food is the most obvious resource and the one most often used in examples, so students generalise it as the sole limiting factor and picture it as a switch rather than a gradually tightening constraint. A population in a culture is limited by several resources and by the build-up of waste. For yeast, glucose supply, ethanol concentration and pH all contribute; for duckweed, mineral ions and surface space matter. Growth slows through a transitional phase as these factors intensify with density.
items.specStatementText: Growing a population in the lab
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is any group of animals living together an example of cooperation?
items.correct: No. Cooperation means individuals act together in a way that benefits each of them, such as pack hunting or shared vigilance. Animals may live in groups while still competing with each other for food, mates or nesting sites.
items.misconception: A herd, flock or shoal is automatically cooperation because the animals are together.
items.why: Being together looks like teamwork, and students have not separated the fact of grouping from the presence of behaviour that benefits the participants. Cooperation is defined by mutual benefit from joint action: wolves hunting in a pack, meerkats acting as sentinels, honeybees foraging for the colony. Members of a grazing herd are still intraspecific competitors for grass.
items.specStatementText: Same species: compete and cooperate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a community include the soil, water and climate of an area?
items.correct: No. A community is the living organisms only; the community together with its abiotic environment is the ecosystem.
items.misconception: A community is everything in the habitat, including the non-living surroundings.
items.why: Students learn 'ecosystem' and 'community' close together and, since both describe 'everything in an area', the abiotic part is attached to the wrong term. Community = all the interacting populations of organisms in an area. Ecosystem = the community plus the abiotic environment with which it interacts.
items.specStatementText: A community is all the living things in an ecosystem
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is any organism that harms another a pathogen?
items.correct: No. Pathogenicity is specifically a microorganism or virus living in a host and causing disease. Harm caused by feeding (parasitism, herbivory, predation) or by chemicals released into the environment is classified differently.
items.misconception: Pathogenicity just means causing harm, so a tick, a walnut tree or a mould that damages other organisms is being a pathogen.
items.why: 'Pathogen' is met as 'something that causes disease', and 'disease' slides into 'harm', so the term is stretched to any damaging relationship. The six categories are distinguished by mechanism. Pathogenicity is disease caused by a microorganism or virus inside a host; parasitism is nutrition taken from a living host; allelopathy and antibiotic secretion are chemicals released to deter competitors.
items.specStatementText: Six ways species interact
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is mutualism one species helping another?
items.correct: No. Mutualism is a relationship in which both species benefit; each partner gains something from the other.
items.misconception: In mutualism one species provides a service to another, which is why it is called 'mutual'; the helper need not gain anything.
items.why: Textbook accounts often describe only the more striking benefit (the bacteria fix nitrogen for the plant, the algae feed the coral), so students remember the relationship as one-directional. For each named example the guide requires the benefits to both organisms: fixed nitrogen for the legume and sugars and shelter for the bacteria; mineral ions and carbon compounds for the orchid and sugars for the fungus; carbon compounds and oxygen for the coral and shelter, carbon dioxide and nitrogen-containing waste for the algae.
items.specStatementText: Mutualism: both partners gain
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are microorganisms living inside plant roots parasites?
items.correct: Not in the cases the guide names. Rhizobium in root nodules and mycorrhizal fungi in orchid roots are mutualists: the plant supplies them with sugars and they supply the plant with fixed nitrogen or with mineral ions and, for orchid seedlings, carbon compounds.
items.misconception: A fungus or bacterium growing inside a plant's roots must be infecting and harming it.
items.why: Fungi and bacteria are mostly encountered as decomposers or as causes of disease, and the sight of hyphae inside root cells looks like an infection. Mycorrhizae in Orchidaceae and root nodules in Fabaceae are mutualisms in which both partners benefit. The plant tolerates and feeds the microorganism because the exchange increases its own growth and, for orchids, is essential for germination.
items.specStatementText: Mutualism: both partners gain
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are endemic species bound to win against introduced species because they are adapted to the local environment?
items.correct: No. An introduced species may have a competitive advantage in resource acquisition, and it often arrives without the predators, pathogens and competitors that limited it in its native range, so it can outcompete endemic species.
items.misconception: Native species are adapted to their habitat, so they must be better at using its resources than a newcomer.
items.why: Adaptation is taught as fitting an organism to its environment, and students infer that the longest-resident species must be the best fitted, overlooking that endemic species are adapted to their existing competitors, not to a new one. Competitive advantage in acquiring resources, not length of residence, decides the outcome. Where the introduced species gains more of a limiting resource per individual, it becomes invasive and the endemic species declines.
items.specStatementText: Invasive species win the competition for resources
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If the calculated chi-squared value is larger than the critical value, is there an association between the species?
items.correct: Yes. A calculated value greater than the critical value (3.84 at p = 0.05 with one degree of freedom) means the difference between observed and expected frequencies is too large to be due to chance, so the null hypothesis of no association is rejected.
items.misconception: A large chi-squared value means the result is unreliable, or means the null hypothesis is accepted.
items.why: Students confuse the chi-squared statistic with the probability value: a small p (below 0.05) is significant, so they assume a small statistic is too. 'Big' is also intuitively associated with 'too much error'. Chi-squared measures how far the observed frequencies are from those expected under the null hypothesis. The larger it is, the less likely the pattern arose by chance; if it exceeds the critical value the association is significant.
items.specStatementText: Chi-squared for association between two species
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Will predators eventually eat all their prey?
items.correct: No. Predation is density-dependent: as prey become scarce the predators find fewer, starve and breed less, so predator numbers fall before the prey are eliminated and the prey population recovers.
items.misconception: Predators keep eating prey until none are left, so prey populations are always heading for extinction.
items.why: Students picture predators as unstoppable consumers and do not connect the predator's own survival and reproduction to the availability of prey. Predator–prey relationships are an example of density-dependent control: the predator population is itself limited by the prey population, which produces oscillations in both rather than extinction.
items.specStatementText: Predator and prey numbers cycle, with the predator lagging
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can top-down and bottom-up control both operate in one community?
items.correct: Yes. Both are possible in any community, although one or the other is likely to be dominant.
items.misconception: A community is controlled either from the top or from the bottom, so evidence for one kind rules the other out.
items.why: The two are taught as contrasting alternatives, and exam questions ask students to pick one, so the idea that both act simultaneously with one dominating is lost. Predators can limit the populations below them at the same time as resource supply limits the producers. The guide's requirement is to understand that both types of control are possible, but that one is likely to be dominant in a given community.
items.specStatementText: Control can come from the top or the bottom
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which direction do the terms top-down and bottom-up refer to?
items.correct: To the trophic level at which the controlling influence originates. Top-down control originates with consumers at higher trophic levels (predators, herbivores) and acts on the levels below; bottom-up control originates with resource supply to producers and acts upward.
items.misconception: The name describes where the affected population is: an effect that ends up at the producers is 'bottom-up', and one that ends up at the predators is 'top-down'.
items.why: The prepositions 'up' and 'down' are read as the destination of the effect rather than its origin, so the terms are reversed. Ask what is doing the controlling. If predators or herbivores are limiting the populations they feed on, control is top-down. If the availability of light, water or mineral nutrients to producers is limiting the community, control is bottom-up.
items.specStatementText: Control can come from the top or the bottom
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does exponential growth mean adding the same number of individuals in each time interval?
items.correct: No. Adding a constant number per interval is linear growth. Exponential growth multiplies the population by a constant factor per interval, so the number added rises as the population rises.
items.misconception: Exponential growth means growth at a constant rate, in the sense of a fixed number of individuals added each interval.
items.why: 'Constant rate' is ambiguous: students take it to mean a fixed number per unit time, as in speed, rather than a fixed proportion per unit time. In exponential growth the population doubles at regular intervals. On ordinary axes this is a curve of increasing steepness; on a logarithmic vertical axis it is a straight line, whereas a fixed number added per interval would give a straight line only on ordinary axes.
items.specStatementText: The sigmoid curve is a model, and real populations can overshoot it
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Under the null hypothesis of independence, do all four cells of a presence/absence contingency table have the same expected frequency?
items.correct: No. Expected frequency for each cell = (row total × column total) ÷ grand total, so it depends on how common each species is. The four cells are equal only when both species each occur in exactly half of the sites.
items.misconception: If two species are distributed independently, each of the four combinations (both, A only, B only, neither) is equally likely, so the expected frequency of every cell is the number of sites divided by four.
items.why: Earlier chi-squared work (dice, coins, Mendelian ratios) supplies expected values from a fixed ratio that is often equal, so 'independent' is read as 'equally likely' and the row and column totals are ignored. Independence means that the presence of one species does not change the chance of the other being present, not that all combinations are equally likely. A species found in 60% of sites is expected in 60% of the sites that contain the other species, which is what (row total × column total) ÷ grand total calculates.
items.specStatementText: Chi-squared for association between two species
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the expected value for the 'both present' cell the probability, or percentage, of sites in which both species occur?
items.correct: No. The chi-squared test compares frequencies, so the expected value is a number of sites: the probability of both being present under independence multiplied by the total number of sites, which equals (row total × column total) ÷ grand total.
items.misconception: The expected value for both species being present is found by multiplying the proportion (or percentage) of sites containing A by the proportion containing B, and that product is what is compared with the observed count.
items.why: In mathematics independence is taught as P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B), a probability, so students stop at the product of the two proportions or percentages and leave out the final multiplication by the number of sites that turns it into a frequency. Multiplying the two proportions gives the expected fraction of sites; multiplying that fraction by the grand total gives the expected number of sites. Since proportion of A = row total ÷ n and proportion of B = column total ÷ n, the result is (row total × column total) ÷ n.
items.specStatementText: Chi-squared for association between two species
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
